myth: Computer chips are made of silicone, the rubbery stuff in kitchen spatulas.
Chips are made of silicon, a hard, shiny grey element found in sand. Silicone is a different, rubbery material that contains silicon mixed with other elements. The names are easy to mix up.

sec.t:
Silicon is the second most common element in [[@earth-layers-crust|Earth's crust]], after oxygen. Most beach and [[@deserts-sand|desert sand]] is quartz, which is silicon joined to oxygen. Chipmakers start with very pure quartz, then heat and treat it to remove almost everything else.

The silicon must be about 99.9999999 percent pure. That is roughly one stray atom in a billion. It is melted, and a small seed crystal is dipped in and slowly pulled up while turning. Silicon freezes onto it in one perfect crystal, a shining grey cylinder that can be taller than a ten-year-old.

Diamond saws slice the crystal into wafers less than a millimetre thick, usually 300 mm across. They are polished until they shine like mirrors.

{{story:glass-made}}

The patterns on a chip are far too small to draw by hand. Instead, the wafer is coated with a light-sensitive chemical. Light shines through a mask, a glass plate carrying the pattern, and the chemical changes where the light lands. The changed areas are washed away, and the uncovered silicon can then be etched or treated.

This is repeated dozens or hundreds of times to build up layers of transistors and wiring. The newest machines, made by the Dutch company ASML, use extreme ultraviolet light and cost well over a hundred million dollars each. Some of the lines they print are only a few dozen atoms wide.

A single speck of dust is like a boulder on a chip's tiny streets. So chips are made in cleanrooms, where air is filtered and pushed down from the ceiling all the time. Workers wear full-body suits, nicknamed bunny suits, with hoods, masks and boots.

Even so, not every chip on a wafer works. Each one is tested. The good ones are cut out and packaged. Some chips that work slightly less well are sold as cheaper, slower models.

The transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs in New Jersey by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley. It replaced bulky glass vacuum tubes and won them the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In 1958 Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit, putting several parts onto one piece of material. Robert Noyce soon made a version on silicon that was easier to mass-produce. The area south of [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] filled with chip companies and became known as [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]].

Today Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced chips. India is building its [[@semiconductors-india|first big chip factories]], including one in Dholera, Gujarat. A modern phone chip, built on the same ideas as those early [[@computers-how|computers]], holds more than 10 billion transistors.

text: Many everyday things began in India. The biggest is the way we write numbers: ten digits, 0 to 9, where a digit's place tells you its value. That system, with [[@zero-invent|zero]] as a real number, was worked out by Indian mathematicians and carried west by Arab scholars.

India also gave the world cotton cloth, an early form of chess, crystal sugar, the board game we call snakes and ladders, and some of the earliest written guides to surgery. [[@inventions-india-modern|In modern times, Indian inventors]] have built [[@prosthetics|cheap artificial legs]], helped invent fibre optics and created a way to send money by phone that the rest of the world now studies.

st.prompt: The English word "shampoo" was borrowed from which language?
st.reveal: It comes from chāmpo, meaning press or knead. In 1814, Sake Dean Mahomed, a traveller from Patna, opened bathhouses in Brighton, England, offering an Indian head massage he called shampooing. The word stuck, though it later came to mean washing hair.

n.certNote: The Indian origin of our place-value digits is well established. Some other claims are less certain. Chess most likely began in India, but a few historians argue for Persia, and the meaning of some very old objects is still debated.

sec.t:
Archaeologists have found traces of cotton thread in the Indus region from over 5,000 years ago. Greek writers who came to India were amazed by a "wool" that grew on trees. For centuries, Indian cloth such as Dhaka muslin was so fine and so prized that it was traded across Asia, Africa and Europe.

By around the Gupta period, Indians had also learned to boil sugarcane juice until it formed crystals. The Sanskrit word khanda, meaning a piece of sugar, is probably where the English word "[[@candy-history|candy]]" comes from.

Two [[@board-games|board games]] also started here. [[@chess-india|Chaturanga]], a battle game with elephants, [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariots]], horses and foot soldiers, most likely grew into [[@pop-chess-pieces|chess]]. Gyan chaupar, a game about good and bad deeds, became [[@snakes-ladders|snakes and ladders]] once it reached Britain.

Indian metalworkers were famous too. From at least around 2,000 years ago, smiths in southern India made a very hard steel called wootz, sealed in small clay pots and heated for hours. Traders carried it to the Middle East, where it was forged into the patterned "Damascus" swords that later impressed European travellers. Modern scientists have studied wootz blades and found tiny structures inside that help explain their strength.

{{story:indus-cities}}

The ancient physician [[@sushruta|Sushruta]] is known for a Sanskrit text that describes many surgical tools and operations. One of them is a way of rebuilding a damaged nose using a flap of skin from the cheek. Doctors still recognise it as an early form of plastic surgery.

A modern example comes from [[@jaipur|Jaipur]]. In 1969, Dr P. K. Sethi and a craftsman named Ram Chandra Sharma designed a rubber artificial foot that was cheap, waterproof and flexible enough to squat, sit cross-legged and walk barefoot. The Jaipur foot has since been fitted for well over a million people around the world, often free of charge.

Narinder Singh Kapany was born in Moga, [[@punjab|Punjab]], in 1926. In the 1950s, working in London and later the United States, he did important early experiments on sending light along thin glass fibres. In 1960 he wrote an article that made the term "fibre optics" popular. Today, glass fibres carry most of the [[@internet-how|internet]]'s data across oceans and cities.

Ajay Bhatt, who grew up in India and later worked at the American company Intel, was one of the team who designed the USB plug used to connect devices.

In 2016, India launched the Unified Payments Interface, or [[@upi-payments|UPI]]. It lets anyone with a bank account and a phone send money instantly by scanning a QR code. A chaiwala on a Pune street corner can take payments as easily as a big shop. Several countries have since signed agreements to use or link with it.

text: The electric telegraph sent messages along wires as bursts of [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. Pressing a key at one end completed a circuit, and a pulse of electric current raced down the wire. At the other end, a machine clicked or made a mark. Short pulses were dots, longer ones were dashes, and patterns of dots and dashes stood for letters. This was [[@codes-morse|Morse code]].

To cross oceans, engineers laid insulated [[@undersea-internet|cables along the sea floor]]. The current travelled through a copper core, protected from seawater by layers of gutta-percha, tarred cloth and iron wire. Messages that once took weeks by ship could arrive in minutes.

st.prompt: In 1858, how long did it take to send Queen Victoria's short message across the first Atlantic telegraph cable?

options.t: About two weeks, the same as a ship

st.reveal: The first cable was weak, and signals came through so faintly that operators had to send each letter slowly and repeat parts. It still beat a ship, which took more than a week. The cable failed within a month.

myth: Samuel Morse invented the telegraph all by himself.

Many people worked on electric telegraphs. In Britain, William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone had a working system in 1837. Morse built on the work of the scientist Joseph Henry, and his partner Alfred Vail helped develop the famous code.

sec.t:
Laying a wire across the Atlantic Ocean was a huge gamble. The first attempts snapped and sank. In 1858 a cable finally linked Ireland to Newfoundland, now part of Canada. Crowds celebrated in New York with [[@fireworks|fireworks]]. Queen Victoria sent a 98-word message to President James Buchanan, and it took about 16 hours to get through.

Then the cable failed after about three weeks. An engineer had pushed too much voltage through it, trying to make the faint signals stronger.

In 1866, the giant steamship Great Eastern, the only vessel big enough to carry the whole cable, laid a stronger one that worked. Within a few decades, cables linked every inhabited continent. News, prices and orders could now cross the planet in a day instead of months.

The telegraph came to India early. In 1851, William O'Shaughnessy, a doctor and scientist working for the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], ran an experimental line from [[@kolkata|Calcutta]] to Diamond Harbour. Within a few years, lines connected Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Agra and Peshawar.

During the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]], the British used the telegraph to send warnings and move troops quickly. Some rebels understood this and cut the wires. A cable to Britain followed in 1870, so messages between London and Bombay took hours rather than the weeks a letter needed.

For more than 150 years, Indians sent telegrams for births, weddings, exams and bad news. Each word cost money, so people wrote in a clipped style: "ARRIVING TUESDAY STOP". India's telegram service sent its last messages on 14 July 2013, after about 162 years.

The telegraph was the first technology to separate communication from transport. Before it, a message could only travel [[@usa-pony-express|as fast as a horse]], a train or a ship carrying it. After it, words moved at nearly the speed of electricity.

Today's undersea cables carry internet data as pulses of light through glass fibres, but many follow routes first mapped by telegraph crews. In that sense, every video call across the ocean travels a road the telegraph built.

text: [[apartheid|Apartheid]] was a system of laws in South Africa that separated people by race and kept power in the hands of the white minority. It began in 1948 and lasted until the early 1990s.

Under apartheid, every person was classified by law as White, Black, Coloured (mixed race) or Indian. Black South Africans, the large majority, were forced into poorer areas, given worse schools, and could not vote for the national government. After years of resistance and pressure from around the world, apartheid was taken apart, and in 1994 [[@nelson-mandela|Nelson Mandela]] became the country's first Black president.

st.prompt: After 21 years of being banned, where did South Africa's cricket team play its first international match in 1991?
st.reveal: South Africa returned to international cricket with a tour of India in November 1991. The first one-day match, at Eden Gardens, drew a huge crowd, a sign of how strongly India had backed the fight against apartheid.

myth: Apartheid ended because the South African government decided on its own that it was wrong.

It ended after decades of protest, strikes, boycotts and armed struggle inside South Africa, together with sanctions and sports bans from around the world. Talks between the government and Mandela's party then set up a new, democratic system.

sec.h: Laws for every part of life
sec.t:
Racial unfairness in South Africa went back to colonial times. Gandhi had fought against it there [[@gandhi-south-africa|as a young lawyer]]. But in 1948 the National Party won the election, with only white people voting, and built a much stricter system.

New laws came one after another. The Population Registration Act put every person into a racial group. The Group Areas Act decided which race could live in each part of a town, and whole neighbourhoods were bulldozed. Black adults had to carry a passbook and show it to police on demand. Beaches, buses, parks and even park benches were marked "Whites only".

Resistance never stopped. The African National Congress (ANC) and other groups organised strikes, boycotts and marches. In 1960, at Sharpeville, police shot dead 69 people protesting against the pass laws. The government banned the ANC, and some members turned to armed struggle.

Mandela was arrested in 1962, and in 1964 he was sentenced to life in prison. He spent 27 years behind bars, 18 of them on Robben Island. Others, such as Archbishop Desmond Tutu, spoke out loudly and won support abroad.

Many countries refused to trade with South Africa or sell it weapons. South Africa was shut out of the Olympics and most international sport, including [[@cricket-history|cricket]] from 1970. Students in the USA and Britain pushed their universities and banks to stop investing there.

India had been one of the earliest and firmest opponents. It cut trade ties in 1946 and spoke against apartheid at the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] for decades.

By the late 1980s, the economy was suffering and the protests were growing. In 1990 President F. W. de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC and freed Mandela. After four tense years of talks, South Africans of all races queued for hours to vote on 27 April 1994, now celebrated as Freedom Day.

A Truth and Reconciliation Commission later let victims tell their stories in public. South Africa's new constitution, adopted in 1996, is often praised as one of the most protective of [[@equality|equal rights]] in the world, though deep gaps in wealth from the apartheid years remain.

text: The Maya and the Aztecs were two great civilisations of Mesoamerica, the region covering much of today's [[@mexico|Mexico]] and Central America. They were different peoples who lived at different times.

The Maya built cities with stone pyramids, palaces and ball courts in the [[@rainforests|rainforests]] of southern Mexico and Central America. They flourished especially from about 250 to 900 CE, and they had a full writing system, advanced mathematics and precise calendars. Maya people did not vanish: millions live in the region today. The Aztecs, who called themselves Mexica, rose much later. In 1325 they founded [[@aztec-tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] on an island in a lake, and built a powerful empire. It fell to Spanish invaders and their local allies in 1521.

st.reveal: The date marked the end of a long period of about 394 years called a b'ak'tun, like a giant odometer rolling over. Maya inscriptions even mention dates far beyond 2012. The "end of the world" idea was a modern invention.

Their calendar simply reached the end of one long cycle on that date. Maya scholars and modern Maya people both say there was no doomsday prophecy.

sec.t:
At its height, the Maya world held dozens of city-states, each ruled by a king. Tikal, in Guatemala, had temple-pyramids rising above the treetops, the tallest about 65 metres high.

Cities fought wars and made alliances. Kings carved their deeds on tall stone slabs called stelae, with dates. Around 900 CE, many great cities in the southern lowlands were abandoned. Historians think a mix of long [[@droughts|droughts]], war and overuse of land played a part. Further north, cities such as Chichen Itza kept going.

The Aztecs arrived in the Valley of Mexico as wanderers. Their legend says their god told them to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus, eating a snake. That image is on Mexico's flag today.

Tenochtitlan grew on an island in Lake Texcoco. Causeways linked it to the shore, and canals ran through it like streets. Farmers built *chinampas*, plots of fertile mud and plants piled up in the shallow lake, where they grew maize, beans and flowers. By 1519, perhaps 2 lakh or more people lived there, more than in any Spanish city of the time.

The Aztecs ruled by demanding tribute, regular payments of goods, from conquered towns: cotton cloth, feathers, cacao beans and more. Cacao beans were so valuable they were used as money.

At the centre of the city stood the Templo Mayor, a great double pyramid for the rain god and the war god. The Aztecs believed the gods needed offerings, including human sacrifice, to keep the Sun moving. This made many neighbouring peoples hate their rule.

In 1519, [[@spanish-conquest|Hernán Cortés]] landed with a few hundred Spanish soldiers. Thousands of Tlaxcalans and other enemies of the Aztecs joined him. A [[@smallpox|smallpox]] [[@disease-history|epidemic]], brought from Europe, killed huge numbers of people who had no immunity to it. In 1521, Tenochtitlan fell.

Mexico City was built on its ruins. Yet Aztec and Maya heritage is everywhere. Words such as chocolate, [[@tomatoes|tomato]] and avocado come from Nahuatl, the Aztec language, which over a million Mexicans still speak.

text: Mahavira was a spiritual teacher who lived in north India around 2,500 years ago, about the same time as the [[@buddha|Buddha]]. He was born Vardhamana, a prince, near Vaishali in [[@bihar-history|Bihar]].

At 30 he gave up his home and possessions to live as a wandering monk. After more than twelve years of hard discipline and meditation, Jains believe he reached perfect knowledge. He then taught for about 30 years. People called him Mahavira, "the great hero", because he had conquered his own desires. His followers are called Jains, and their most important teaching is [[ahimsa|ahimsa]], not harming any living being.

st.reveal: Uprooting a plant ends its life completely, and digging disturbs many small living things in the soil. Many Jains avoid root vegetables so they cause as little harm as possible. Practices vary between families.

sec.h: A prince who gave everything away
sec.t:
According to Jain tradition, Vardhamana grew up in comfort. One version of his story says he waited until his parents had died, then left home with his elder brother's permission.

Jains believe he walked from village to village for twelve and a half years, often fasting, speaking little and enduring heat, cold and insults. Jain traditions say that in time he gave up even his clothes. At 42, sitting under a sal tree on a riverbank, he reached *kevala jnana*, which Jains understand as complete, all-seeing knowledge.

Jain monks and nuns take five great vows: not to harm, not to lie, not to steal, to stay celibate, and not to own things. Ordinary Jains follow gentler forms of the same vows.

The last one, *aparigraha*, means not clinging to possessions. Jains believe that owning too much ties you down, just as harming others does. Many Jain families are known for giving generously to animal shelters, hospitals and schools. In Delhi, a Jain bird hospital near the Red Fort has treated injured [[@urban-wildlife|pigeons]], sparrows and other birds for decades.

Mahavira also taught *anekantavada*, the idea that truth has many sides and no single view captures all of it.

Jains often explain it with the story of several blind men touching an elephant. One feels the trunk and says it's a snake. Another feels a leg and says it's a tree trunk. Each is partly right and none is wholly right. The story is told in Buddhist and Hindu traditions too, and it is a gentle reminder to listen before arguing.

Mahavira died at 72 at Pavapuri in Bihar. Jains celebrate his birth on Mahavir Jayanti, and his final liberation on [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]].

Jainism has stayed fairly small, with about 45 lakh followers in India in 2011, but its influence is wide. At Shravanabelagola in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], a 17-metre statue of the Jain saint Bahubali, carved from a single rock more than 1,000 years ago, draws pilgrims from across India. Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] grew up in Gujarat among Jain neighbours and friends, and his idea of fighting without violence owes something to Mahavira's ahimsa.

text: The Mayflower was an English merchant ship that carried 102 passengers across the Atlantic Ocean in 1620. About a third belonged to a religious group who had broken away from the Church of England. They wanted to worship in their own way, and had lived for years in the Netherlands before deciding to start again in America. The rest were other settlers hoping for land and work.

They landed on the coast of what is now Massachusetts, on the homeland of the Wampanoag people, and founded Plymouth Colony. They are now called the Pilgrims. Their story is told every year in the United States at [[@thanksgiving|Thanksgiving]].

st.reveal: Records of their belongings list clothes in many colours. Black was for Sundays and special days, and it was expensive to dye. The buckles came from artists painting them 200 years later.

Ask your class to stand inside it, then remember that over 130 people, plus cargo and animals, shared a ship like that for over two months.
myth: The Pilgrims stepped ashore onto Plymouth Rock.

sec.t:
The group had planned to sail in two ships, but the second one, the Speedwell, leaked so badly that it turned back. Everyone squeezed onto the Mayflower, which left Plymouth in England in September 1620.

The ship was probably about 30 metres long, roughly one and a half cricket pitches. Passengers lived in the dark, cramped space between decks for about two months. It relied entirely on the wind, like all [[@boats-sail|sailing ships]] of its day, and autumn gales battered it. At one point a main beam cracked. They fixed it with a large iron screw they had brought along, perhaps from a printing press. A baby named Oceanus Hopkins was born at sea.

The settlers began building at Plymouth in December, but they arrived too late to plant crops. Many lived on the ship through the cold. Disease spread, probably made worse by poor food and the long voyage. About half the passengers died before spring.

The land was not empty. It was Patuxet, a Wampanoag village whose people had been nearly wiped out by an epidemic, probably brought by earlier European visitors, a few years before.

In March 1621 a Native man named Samoset walked into the settlement and greeted them in English, which he had learned from fishermen. He returned with Tisquantum, often called Squanto, who had been kidnapped and taken to Europe years earlier and had learned English there. He showed the settlers how to plant maize with fish as fertiliser.

The Wampanoag leader Massasoit, also known as Ousamequin, agreed an alliance with the colonists. Each side promised to help the other against enemies. Both had reasons: the Wampanoag had been weakened by disease and faced rival nations.

That autumn, after their first harvest, the colonists held a celebration. About 90 Wampanoag men joined them, and the gathering lasted three days. They ate deer the Wampanoag brought, along with wild birds and other food. There is no record of pumpkin pie.

Peace between the two peoples lasted about 50 years. Then, as more settlers took more land, it broke down into a bloody war in 1675. For many Wampanoag and other Native people today, Thanksgiving is a day of mourning as well as memory. Their [[@native-nations|nation]] still lives in Massachusetts.

text: A desert is a place that gets very little rain or snow, usually less than about 250 mm a year. That is less than many Indian cities get in a single monsoon month. By that measure, the biggest desert on Earth is Antarctica, at about 14 million square kilometres, followed by [[@arctic|the Arctic]].

The biggest hot desert is the [[@sahara|Sahara]], in North Africa, at about 9.2 million square kilometres. After that come the Arabian Desert, the Gobi in [[@mongolia|Mongolia]] and China, the Kalahari in southern Africa, and the great deserts of Australia. Deserts cover roughly a third of all the land on Earth. Many of them are rocky, not sandy, and some are bitterly cold.

st.reveal: A desert is defined by how little rain or snow falls, not by heat or sand. Antarctica gets so little that it counts as a desert, and at about 14 million square kilometres it is the biggest of all. The Arctic comes next, and the Sahara third.

sec.h: Why some places get no rain
sec.t:
Deserts form for a few reasons. Many, like the Sahara and Arabian, lie along belts about 20 to 30 degrees north and south of the equator. There, air that rose over the hot, wet tropics sinks again, warming up and drying out as it falls. Sinking dry air means clear skies and very little rain.

Some deserts sit behind tall mountains, which block rain clouds. Others, like the Atacama in Chile, are next to cold [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]] that cool the air and stop it from forming rain clouds. Antarctica's air is so cold it can hardly hold any moisture at all.

The Atacama Desert, a narrow strip along the coast of Chile and Peru, is the driest hot desert on Earth. Some weather stations there have gone years without measurable rain. Its soil is so dry and lifeless in places that NASA has tested equipment for [[@mars-rovers|Mars rovers]] there, because it is one of the most [[@mars-colonies|Mars-like]] spots on our planet.

Yet the Atacama is not completely empty. Fog from the sea rolls in on some mornings. People have set up big nets to catch fog droplets for water. When rare rains do come, the desert can burst into flower, carpeting the sand in pink and purple.

India's largest desert, the [[@thar-formed|Thar]], covers much of western Rajasthan and stretches into Pakistan. It is home to the cities of Jaisalmer, Bikaner and Jodhpur, and is one of the most crowded deserts in the world, with many towns and villages.

People there have adapted carefully. They store rainwater in tanks, build homes with thick walls to stay cool, and raise [[@camels|camels]], goats and hardy crops like millet. Folk music, bright turbans and mirrorwork cloth are part of desert life.

The south-west United States has several deserts, including the Mojave and the Sonoran. The Sonoran Desert is home to the saguaro cactus, which can grow over 12 m tall and live for over 150 years.

[[@mystery-sailing-stones|Death Valley]], in the Mojave Desert, holds the [[@weather-records|record for the hottest]] air temperature ever officially measured. It shows that deserts can be extreme in both directions: burning by day, and sometimes surprisingly cold at night.

text: Switzerland is a small country in the middle of Europe, with no coast. About 60 percent of it is covered by the Alps, with peaks over 4,000 metres, glaciers, deep valleys and lakes. Mountains made Switzerland hard to invade, hard to farm and hard to cross, and the Swiss became experts at living with them: [[@extreme-longest-tunnels|building tunnels]], railways and mountain villages.

Clocks and watches came from a different kind of hard work. In the long winters, farmers in the Jura mountains made watch parts at home. Over centuries, Swiss workshops became famous for tiny, precise machines that keep time. Switzerland is also known for chocolate, [[@food-why-cheese-holes|cheese]], banks, peace talks and the red flag with a white cross.

st.prompt: Where do cuckoo clocks, often sold as Swiss souvenirs, actually come from?
st.reveal: Cuckoo clocks were developed in the Black Forest region of south-west Germany in the 1700s. Switzerland's great tradition is precision watches, not carved wooden cuckoo clocks.

d.try: Make a simple pendulum. Tie a small weight, like a key or a washer, to a string about 25 cm long and hang it from a table edge. Count how many swings it makes in 30 seconds. Then halve the string's length and count again. Pendulums like this kept time in clocks for centuries.

sec.t:
The Matterhorn, a sharp pyramid of rock, rises to 4,478 metres above the village of Zermatt. It is the peak you may have seen on postcards and calendars. The highest point in the country is the Dufourspitze, at 4,634 metres. Glaciers fill the high valleys, but they are shrinking fast. Swiss scientists report that the country's [[@glaciers|glaciers]] lost about a tenth of their remaining ice in just 2022 and 2023.

Indian audiences know these mountains well. From the 1970s onwards, film-makers such as Yash Chopra shot romantic [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] songs in Swiss meadows and lakes. Indian tourists followed, and in 2016 a statue of Yash Chopra was put up in Interlaken.

In the 1500s, the religious reformer John Calvin led the city of Geneva. Its strict rules banned showy jewellery. Goldsmiths needed new work, so many turned to making watches, which counted as useful rather than vain.

The skills spread into the Jura mountains, where towns like La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle were even laid out around watchmaking workshops. In the 1970s, cheap [[@minerals-everyday|quartz]] watches from Japan nearly wiped out the Swiss industry. It fought back in 1983 with the Swatch, a colourful plastic watch. Today Swiss watches are sold all over the world, and their tiny gears show how [[@clocks|clocks]] turn a steady beat into hours and minutes. Cuckoo clocks, though, are not Swiss at all. They come from the Black Forest, just over the border in Germany.

Swiss chocolate has a similar story of clever tinkering. In 1875, Daniel Peter of Vevey mixed in condensed milk made by his neighbour Henri Nestlé and created one of the first successful milk chocolates. A few years later, Rodolphe Lindt invented a machine that stirred chocolate for days until it turned silky. That is how [[@chocolate-making|chocolate making]] went from gritty to smooth.

{{story:web-invented}}

Getting across the Alps has always been hard. Today trains do it underground. The Gotthard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016, runs for 57 kilometres under the mountains. It is the longest railway [[@tunnels|tunnel]] in the world, and freight and passenger trains race through it at up to about 200 km/h.

Above ground, mountain trains climb with cogwheels that grip a toothed rail. The Jungfrau railway reaches a station at about 3,450 metres, the highest in Europe.

sec.h: Four languages and a lot of voting
sec.t:
Switzerland has four national languages: German in most of the north and centre, French in the west, Italian in the south and Romansh in a few mountain valleys. Many Swiss speak two or three.

Swiss citizens vote on national questions several times a year, from taxes to railways. This direct form of [[@democracy-what|democracy]] lets citizens propose new laws themselves. Switzerland has also stayed neutral in wars since 1815, and Geneva hosts the [[@red-cross|Red Cross]] and many United Nations offices. In 1989, at the [[@extreme-biggest-machines|CERN laboratory]] near Geneva, [[@hist-first-website|Tim Berners-Lee]] wrote the proposal that led to the [[@web-invented|World Wide Web]].

text: Arabic is written right to left because it inherited that direction from older scripts of the Middle East. The Phoenician alphabet, the Aramaic script and the Hebrew script were all written right to left. Arabic grew out of a form of Aramaic used by the Nabataeans, the people who built the rock city of [[@petra|Petra]] in Jordan, and kept the same direction.

Why those first scripts ran right to left is less certain. One popular idea is that early writers carved stone with a chisel in the left hand and a hammer in the right, which made working leftwards natural. Others point to writing on clay or with ink. Nobody has proved any of these, and most experts say we simply don't know.

st.prompt: In an Arabic newspaper, words run right to left. Which way do you read a number like 2025?

options.t: Left to right, just as in English
Right to left, so it says 5202

st.reveal: Numbers in Arabic text are read from left to right, starting with the biggest place value, just as in English and Hindi. A reader's eyes move right to left through the words, then jump to the left end of a number to read it.

The British Library, Arabic scripts and manuscripts.

n.certNote: Arabic clearly inherited its right-to-left direction from older Middle Eastern scripts. Why those very first scripts ran right to left is not known for sure, and the popular explanations are guesses.

sec.t:
The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters. Most join to the letters next to them, so a word looks like one flowing line. Because of this, a letter can change shape depending on whether it comes at the start, middle or end of a word, or stands alone.

Arabic is mostly an abjad, a kind of writing that shows consonants but not every vowel. Short vowels can be added as small marks above or below the letters, as in the [[@quran-intro|Quran]] and in children's schoolbooks. Everyday writing usually leaves them out, and readers fill them in from context, the way "txt msgs" can still be read.

The Arabic script spread with Islam and trade, from the 600s onwards, across the Middle East, North Africa and Central and South Asia. Many languages adopted it and added letters for sounds Arabic does not have. Persian, Pashto, Kashmiri and Sindhi all use forms of it.

In India and Pakistan, [[@urdu|Urdu]] is written in a flowing style called Nastaliq, which slopes downward from right to left. Arabic itself became one of the official languages of the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] in 1973. Turkish was written in Arabic script until 1928, when Turkey switched to Latin letters. After the Latin alphabet, the Arabic script is used by more of the world's countries than any other.

Because Islamic tradition avoided pictures of people in religious places, [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]] became one of its greatest arts. Verses were carved in stone, painted on tiles and woven into carpets. Styles range from the square, angular Kufic to the rounded Naskh used in most printed books.

You can see [[@calligraphy-world|Arabic calligraphy]] across India too. The [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]]'s great gateway and walls are framed with verses from the Quran, inlaid in black stone. The lettering was designed to look the same size from the ground all the way up, so the letters near the top are larger.

The digits 0 to 9 began in India, where mathematicians were using a place-value system with [[@zero-invent|zero]] by about 1,400 years ago. Arab and Persian scholars learned them, and al-Khwarizmi of Baghdad wrote a famous book about them around 825 CE. Europeans then learned the digits from Arabic books and called them [[@indian-numerals|Arabic numerals]].

Many Arab countries today use a different set of digit shapes, sometimes called Eastern Arabic numerals. But in both systems, numbers are still written with the biggest place first, on the left.

text: It depends how you count. In the 2011 census, Indians named 19,569 different mother tongues. Many were the same language under different names, or local [[dialect|dialects]]. After grouping them, the census listed 121 languages spoken by at least 10,000 people each.

India's Constitution gives special recognition to 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, from Assamese to Urdu. Hindi and English are used for the work of the central government, and each state chooses its own official languages.
A separate count, the People's Linguistic Survey of India, found about 780 languages. Whichever number you pick, India is one of the most linguistically varied countries on Earth.

st.prompt: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of India's Constitution?
st.reveal: The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages, from Assamese to Urdu. The list started with 14 in 1950 and has grown since. India speaks many more languages than this, but these have special recognition.

src: Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, Census of India 2011, language data.

People's Linguistic Survey of India, led by G. N. Devy.
n.certNote: There is no single answer. The count depends on where you draw the line between a language and a dialect, and different surveys use different rules.

d.try: Make a language map of your class or building. Ask each person which languages their family speaks at home, at school and with grandparents. Draw a chart with a bar for each language. Count how many people speak two or more. You may be surprised how many languages share one corridor.
myth: Everyone in India speaks Hindi.

Hindi is the most spoken language, but in 2011 well over half of Indians named a different mother tongue. Many people in the south and north-east speak little or no Hindi, using their state language and English instead.

sec.t:
Most Indian languages belong to four families, groups of languages descended from a common ancestor. Indo-Aryan languages, such as Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati and Punjabi, are spoken across the north, west and east. Dravidian languages, including [[@tamil-ancient|Tamil]], Telugu, Kannada and [[@malayalam|Malayalam]], are spoken mostly in the south.

Austroasiatic languages include Santali and Mundari in central and eastern India and Khasi in Meghalaya. Tibeto-Burman languages, such as Bodo, Manipuri and many Naga languages, are spoken across the Himalaya and the north-east.

A few languages fit no family at all. Nihali, spoken by a small community on the border of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, seems unrelated to any other language. On the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]], the Great Andamanese languages now have only a handful of speakers.

After independence, people in many regions asked for states based on the language they spoke. In 1952, Potti Sriramulu fasted for a separate Telugu-speaking state and died after 58 days without food. His death led to the creation of Andhra State in 1953. Three years later, the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew much of India's map along language lines.

That is why Karnataka is largely Kannada-speaking, [[@kerala|Kerala]] largely Malayalam-speaking, and so on. It is also why an ordinary Indian banknote is a small lesson in languages, with its value printed in 15 of them on a panel at the back.

Some of India's languages have tens of millions of speakers. Others have only a few hundred, often elders in a single village. When children stop learning a language, it can vanish within a generation, taking songs, stories and knowledge of local plants and animals with it. In 2009, UNESCO listed nearly 200 Indian languages as vulnerable or endangered.

Communities are fighting back. Santali now has its own script, Ol Chiki, created in 1925 by Raghunath Murmu, and is taught in schools. Linguists are recording elders' speech, and young people are making videos, songs and dictionaries in their own [[@endangered-languages|endangered languages]].

text: Libraries began soon after writing did. In ancient [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], temples and palaces kept collections of clay tablets: records, prayers, laws, stories and lists of words. As kingdoms grew, rulers collected texts to look powerful and wise.

For most of history, libraries were private. They belonged to kings, temples, monasteries and [[@hist-first-university|universities]], and only a few scholars could use them. Public libraries, open to anyone for free, are a much newer idea, mostly from the last 200 years.

st.prompt: King Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, about 2,700 years old, held thousands of texts. What were they written on?
st.reveal: Scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into soft clay. When the palace was destroyed in 612 BCE, the fire baked many tablets harder. The British Museum now holds tens of thousands of tablets and fragments from Nineveh.

n.certNote: We know a lot about some ancient libraries from finds and records. Others, like the Library of Alexandria, are surrounded by legends, and historians still argue about how big they were and how they ended.

myth: The Library of Alexandria was destroyed in one great fire.
Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE may have burned some books, but most historians think the library faded slowly over centuries, as funding stopped and the city went through wars.

Father of library science in India

sec.t:
In the 600s BCE, King Ashurbanipal of Assyria gathered a huge library at his capital, Nineveh, in today's northern Iraq. He sent scribes across his empire to copy texts on medicine, astronomy, magic, history and poetry. One copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh, among the world's oldest stories, comes from there.

The tablets were written in cuneiform, a script of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay. Many ended with a short note, called a colophon, saying that they belonged to the king. In 612 BCE enemies sacked Nineveh. Its tablets lay buried until archaeologists dug them up in the 1800s, and many are now in the British Museum in London.

About 300 BCE, the Greek rulers of Egypt founded a great library at Alexandria. They wanted a copy of every important book in the known world. A famous story says ships in the harbour had their books copied, and the owners were given back copies while the library kept the originals.

Nobody knows exactly how many scrolls it held. Numbers from ancient writers vary wildly, and the [[@great-libraries|great lost libraries]] attract plenty of legends.

In India, the Buddhist university of [[@nalanda|Nalanda]] in Bihar had a famous library, remembered by the name Dharmaganja. Students and monks came from [[@china-today|China]], Korea and Tibet to study and copy texts on palm leaves. Nalanda was attacked and ruined around 1200 CE, and much of its learning was lost. Its ruins are now a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site.

{{story:great-libraries}}

Libraries open to the public grew as printing made books cheaper. In 1731, Benjamin Franklin and friends in Philadelphia set up the Library Company, where members shared the cost of books. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, the American businessman Andrew Carnegie paid for more than 2,500 library buildings around the world.

The Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., was founded in 1800. British troops burned the Capitol, and the library inside it, in 1814. [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]] sold Congress his personal collection to rebuild it. Today it is one of the largest libraries in the world, with well over 100 million items.

A big library is useless if nobody can find anything. In 1876, the American librarian Melvil Dewey published a system that gives every subject a number, using [[@decimals|decimals]] to split topics more finely. Science books might sit in the 500s, with animals around 590.

In India, the mathematician-librarian S. R. Ranganathan invented another system, Colon Classification, and wrote the Five Laws of Library Science in 1931. The first is simple: "Books are for use." His birthday, 12 August, is celebrated as National Librarians' Day in India.

Today, libraries also lend e-books, offer computers and help people sort good information from bad. A modern library catalogue works a bit like a [[@search-engines|search engine]], but every entry was checked by a person.

text: Fermentation is what happens when [[microbe|microbes]], living things too small to see, feed on the sugars in food. As they eat, they give off waste. Luckily for us, that waste is often delicious.

Some microbes make acids, which give curd and [[@pickles-achar|pickles]] their tang and stop harmful germs from growing. Some make bubbles of gas, which lift bread and idli. Some make alcohol, which is how grape juice becomes wine. People have used fermentation for thousands of years, long before anyone knew microbes existed.

st.prompt: Idli batter is often much puffier in the morning than it was at night. What made it rise?

options.t: Microbes ate sugars in the batter and gave off gas
The rice grains slowly soaked up air from the kitchen
The salt in the batter grew into crystals

st.reveal: Bacteria and yeasts living on the rice and urad dal feed overnight. They make bubbles of carbon dioxide, which puff the batter up, and acids, which give idli its gentle sour taste.

d.try: Mix two spoons of wheat flour with two spoons of water in a clean glass jar. Cover it loosely with a cloth, then add a spoon of each every day. Within a few days you should see bubbles and smell something sour. Do not eat it; just watch the microbes at work.
myth: All bacteria are harmful germs.
Only a small share of bacteria make people ill. Many are harmless, and some are useful, like the ones that turn milk into curd or that help digest food in your gut.

sec.t:
Put a spoon of old curd into warm milk and leave it overnight. By morning the milk has set. The spoon of curd carried millions of lactic acid [[bacteria|bacteria]]. They feed on lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and make lactic acid.

The acid makes milk [[protein|proteins]] clump together into a soft, wobbly gel, and it gives [[@curd-yogurt|curd]] its tangy taste. Acid also makes life hard for many harmful germs, which is one reason curd keeps longer than fresh milk. Yogurt in the United States is made the same way, with closely related bacteria.

South Indian [[@dosa-idli|idli and dosa]] batter is a mix of ground rice and urad dal, left to sit overnight. Bacteria and wild [[yeast|yeasts]] living on the grains get to work. They puff the batter with gas and give it a light sourness.

Bread works the same way. Bakers mix yeast into dough, and as it feeds, it breathes out carbon dioxide that makes the [[@food-science-bread-rise|dough rise]]. In sourdough bread, made in [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] and many other places, wild yeasts and bacteria work together, like a tiny team that has been passed from loaf to loaf for years.

Fermented foods are everywhere. [[@seoul|Korean]] kimchi, German sauerkraut, [[@soybeans|Japanese soy sauce]], vinegar, many cheeses and the kanji drink of north India all rely on microbes. Even [[@chocolate-making|chocolate]] starts this way: cacao beans are piled up and left to ferment for days, which builds up the flavours that later become chocolate.

Not every sour, long-lasting food is fermented, though. Many Indian pickles, or achar, keep for months mainly because of salt, oil and spices, which make it hard for spoiling microbes to grow. Others, like some carrot and mustard pickles, are left in the sun so that friendly bacteria can sour them slowly. Cooks learned which method suited which vegetable by trial and error over many generations.

The same idea shows up in [[@food-why-cheese-holes|cheese]]. Cheese makers add bacteria, and sometimes moulds, to milk curds, then leave them to age for weeks or years. Each mix of microbes gives a different smell and flavour. Paneer is different: it is set with lemon juice or vinegar and eaten fresh, with no ageing at all.

Scientists are now studying how eating fermented foods affects the [[@microbes-friendly|friendly microbes]] in our [[@digestion-gut|gut]]. Early results are interesting but not settled. What is clear is that people across the world, with no microscopes at all, learned to team up with creatures they could not see.

text: Your [[@immune-system|immune system]] is your body's defence force. It hunts down germs and attacks them. In someone with a food allergy, it makes a mistake. It treats a harmless [[protein|protein]] in a food, such as [[@peanut-butter|peanut]], milk or egg, as if it were a dangerous invader.

The next time that person eats the food, the immune system sounds the alarm. Cells release chemicals such as [[histamine|histamine]], which can cause itchy skin, swelling, [[@digestion-gut|stomach pain]] or vomiting. In a severe reaction called anaphylaxis, the throat can swell and breathing can become hard. That is a medical emergency.

st.prompt: Peanuts are one of the most common food allergies. What kind of plant is a peanut?

options.t: A legume, like lentils and peas
A tree nut, like almonds and cashews
A grain, like wheat and rice

st.reveal: Peanuts grow in pods underground, just as peas grow in pods above ground. They are legumes. Someone allergic to peanuts is not always allergic to tree nuts, and the other way round, though some people are allergic to both.

myth: Peanuts are nuts.
Peanuts are legumes, related to beans, peas and lentils. Almonds, cashews and walnuts are called tree nuts. Doctors treat the two as separate allergies.

milk, egg, peanut, tree nuts, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, sesame

sec.t:
Not every bad reaction to food is an allergy. Many people cannot digest lactose, the sugar in milk, and get a tummy ache or gas after drinking it. That is lactose intolerance. It is uncomfortable, but it does not involve the immune system and is not dangerous in the same way.

A true allergy can be serious, so it is important to find out which is which. If a food seems to make you unwell, tell a trusted adult. A doctor can test for allergies safely.

People with serious food allergies often carry an adrenaline auto-injector. It is a pen-shaped device that pushes medicine into the thigh. [[@hormones|Adrenaline]], also called epinephrine, quickly opens the airways and keeps blood pressure up. After using it, the person still needs to go to hospital.

Many schools in the United States keep these pens and train staff. Knowing the warning signs, like swelling lips or trouble breathing, is a useful part of [[@first-aid|first aid]] for anyone.

For years, parents of babies at risk of allergies were told to avoid peanuts. In 2015 a large study in London, called LEAP, tested the opposite. Babies at high risk who were given small amounts of peanut food from early in life were about 80% less likely to develop a peanut allergy by age five.

That changed advice in the US and UK. Doctors now often suggest introducing peanut foods early, under medical guidance for high-risk babies. It is a reminder that common sense is not always right, and careful tests matter.

Children with serious food allergies learn to live carefully, but they can still do almost everything their friends do. They read labels, ask how food was cooked and sometimes carry their own snacks to parties. Packaged foods in the US must clearly list major allergens, and sesame was added to that list in 2023.

Friends can help too. Not sharing food without asking and knowing who to tell in an emergency make a real difference. Some children grow out of milk and egg allergies as they get older, while peanut allergies more often last.

Food allergies appear to have become more common in many countries over recent decades. Scientists are not sure why. One idea is that children today meet fewer of the [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]] that once trained the immune system. Others point to changes in diet, vitamin D or how early babies try foods.

India has less research. Peanuts are a common snack there, and some doctors think peanut allergy is less frequent than in the US, but there is not enough data to be sure.

text: Tex-Mex is the cooking of [[@texas|Texas]] that grew out of Mexican food. It was created mainly by Tejanos, Texans of Mexican descent, and then shaped by American tastes and American shops.

You can usually spot Tex-Mex by a few clues. There is plenty of melted yellow cheese, a lot of beef, a warm, earthy flavour of cumin, and soft wheat-flour tortillas or crunchy fried shells. Famous dishes include chili con carne, nachos, fajitas, crispy tacos and a bowl of melted cheese dip called queso. It is a border cuisine, born where two countries, two languages and two kitchens rub against each other.

st.prompt: In 1943, a waiter in a small Mexican town made the first nachos for some visiting American women. What was the waiter's name?
st.reveal: Ignacio "Nacho" Anaya cut tortillas into triangles, fried them, and topped them with cheese and jalapeño slices. The dish took his nickname, and it spread across Texas and beyond.

Tex-Mex grew up in Texas and has its own habits, such as lots of yellow cheese, beef, cumin and wheat-flour tortillas. Many dishes from different regions of Mexico taste quite different and are rarely seen in Tex-Mex restaurants.

sec.t:
Before 1836, Texas belonged to [[@mexico|Mexico]]. After a war that year it became an independent republic, and in 1845 it joined the United States. Many families who had lived there for generations suddenly found themselves in a new country without moving an inch.

They kept cooking what they knew, using what they could find. Beef was cheap on the great cattle ranches of Texas, and wheat flour was easy to buy. So beef crept into dishes that might have used pork or chicken, and flour tortillas sat beside corn ones.

sec.h: The chili queens of San Antonio

sec.t:
In 1943, a group of American women from a nearby army base crossed the border into Piedras Negras, a Mexican town across the river from Eagle Pass, Texas. The cook was away. The head waiter, Ignacio Anaya, went into the kitchen and grabbed what he had.

He cut tortillas into triangles, fried them, added cheese and slices of jalapeño chilli, and warmed them until the cheese melted. He called the plate "Nacho's especiales". The dish crossed back over the border and is now eaten in cinemas from Mumbai to Miami.

Fajitas began on Texas ranches, where Mexican cowboys, called vaqueros, were often paid partly in the cheapest cuts of beef. One was skirt steak, a thin strip from below the ribs. Grilled fast over fire and wrapped in a tortilla, it became a meal. Restaurants made fajitas popular in the 1970s, served sizzling on a hot iron plate.

Tex-Mex is a kind of fusion: a new cuisine made when two food traditions meet. India has its own famous example. [[@chinese-food-india|Indo-Chinese food]], with dishes such as gobi Manchurian, grew up in Kolkata and Mumbai and is quite unlike food in China. Both were made by people far from their original homes, cooking for neighbours with new tastes.

Indian visitors to a Tex-Mex restaurant often notice familiar things: rajma-like beans, green chillies and the smell of jeera, which is cumin. It turns out that a plate of nachos and a plate of chole have more in common than you might guess.
